question.prompt: What is the size of the largest subset \(S\) of \(\{1,2,3,\ldots,50\}\) such that no pair of distinct elements of \(S\) has a sum divisible by \(7?\)

solutions.explanation:
Whether a sum is divisible by \(7\) depends only on the two remainders after division by \(7\). Grouping the numbers by these remainders makes the restrictions independent.

Among \(1,2,\ldots,49\), each remainder \(0,1,\ldots,6\) occurs seven times. The remaining number, \(50\), has remainder \(1\). Thus the remainder-\(1\) class has eight elements, while every other class has seven.

The nonzero remainders pair as
\[
(1,6),\qquad(2,5),\qquad(3,4).
\]
We cannot select numbers from both classes of any pair, because their sum would have remainder \(0\). These three pairs therefore contribute at most \(8\), \(7\), and \(7\) elements, respectively. Also, two distinct multiples of \(7\) have a sum divisible by \(7\), so we may select at most one of them. Since these groups include every number, this proves
\[
|S|\le 8+7+7+1=23.
\]
To achieve the bound, take every number with remainder \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\), together with the number \(7\). Two chosen nonmultiples have remainder sum between \(2\) and \(6\), and adding \(7\) to one of them preserves its nonzero remainder. There is only one selected multiple of \(7\), so every pair of distinct selected numbers is allowed.

This set has \(\boxed{23}\) elements, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutions.title: Pair complementary remainders
